answer.evidence: The tile is a ramp seen from the south. Rows 0-63 show an inclined olive ramp plane with a chevron texture. It is flanked by brown block cliff walls, a dark one at the left and a lighter one at the right. The left wall's inner edge steps inward toward the bottom, rows 4-62, so it reads as a receding wall face. Rows 64-79 are flat olive ground with no edge line or shadow. No row has a front-edge line or eave shadow, and there is no standing front face, because the cliff is drawn only as the side walls. It is terrain, not a standing object, so the top/front rules fit only loosely and I report it as 'other'.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are fine for the candidate: 10 visible tones per tile against 3 for the grass and 7 for the paving, and only 12% neutral dark edges, so the dark brown side walls and edges lean toward the material tone rather than a black line. The picture is weaker than the numbers. The ramp is built from a few chevron bands of olive-yellow, each close to a flat fill with only a thin highlight and shadow line. The lower landing is a large, nearly uniform tan block with no grain, tufts or per-pixel variation. That matches the 20% near-flat coverage, where both references have 0%. The main ramp material shows about 4 lightness steps, below Beodeul's 5-6. The surface reads as banded and graphic rather than carrying the speckle and grain of the references. When in doubt, fail.
